owner: CC (code+proofs); Akien (the design ruling: one ticket both halves, post-build inspector NOT an overnight scan, 2026-07-29)
intention: WORK NEVER RIDES LOOSE — durability becomes physics at TWO EVENTS and no clock. (1) THE CROSSING: a new build_inspector SIEVE (`working_tree_clean`) reds a component whose own subtree carries uncommitted changes, so a stone cannot be promoted out of PROVEME while the code it claims exists only in a working tree. (2) THE BOUNDARY: /saveslate stops being hand-authored JSON and gets a write door that measures both roots by instrument, makes any dirt durable (commit + push) BEFORE writing the slate, and records the resulting shas in the slate itself — so a continuity record can never outlive the work it describes.
why: The durability gate has been a bound, unbuilt gate since 2026-07-15: node_classes/code-seam.json `extra_gates` reads 'a code-seam is not done until tested AND durably committed (git). Durability-of-stones sits on the emit chokepoint (physics), not a step anyone remembers to run.' skills/commit/intention+why.json says the same from the other side: 'a skill invented to force a behavior is policy standing in for a missing gate.' Both have been pointing at this stone for two weeks. Today it came due from the far end: /saveslate wrote slate 2026-07-29-resume-opus-inline while SEVEN files of stone C's berth-work sat uncommitted in cairn and one in CairnCommons. The slate named the dirty files honestly and was still the wrong artifact — a durable record whose pointer resolved to a working tree, which a dead box resolves to nothing. That is Law 1's most expensive failure: not re-deriving a settled answer, but re-deriving a BUILT one. build_inspector's own growth rule already claims this case in its charter: 'a failure Akien catches that a sieve could have caught becomes a sieve, and the class stops recurring.' Akien caught it. A sieve could have caught it.
traces_to: Law 4 — the whole point: 'commit before you stop' in an operator's habit is policy; a sieve at the crossing and a door at the boundary are physics. This stone discharges the durability IOU named in code-seam.json extra_gates and skills/commit/intention+why.json, both dated 2026-07-15
Law 1 — uncommitted proven work that must be rebuilt is re-deriving the SETTLED at its most expensive; the defect Law 1 exists to stop
Law 3 — the slate's own charter says 'a slate that names a file is a pointer to verify, not a proof'; a sha IS checkable, so the durability field turns that line from hypothesis into measurement
Law 8 — a stone promoted with its code only in a working tree is a hollow pass: the proof ran against bytes nothing durable holds

the founding intention (get Akien out of running the system) — 'commit when Akien has asked' put him back in the operator seat; the asymmetry is the argument: an unnecessary commit costs a line of history, an uncommitted one can cost the work
state: code-seam@v2: THINKME -> TICKETME -> [BUILDME] -> PROVEME -> PROVED   (cast 2026-07-29; leaf, so TICKETME is skippable per the class's skippable_summons; chart pending — the entry gate demands a berthed chart chain before BUILDME)
gates: proof gate: teeth beside the code, under the tester with the netns seal. THE CROSSING HALF (cairn/machines/build_inspector/proofs/test_inspector.py): the new sieve fires on a synthetic component with seeded dirt and stays quiet on a clean one (tooth 1 + tooth 2, the founding fire-and-stay-quiet pair); it carries its seeding failure as docstring Provenance (tooth 10 refuses a sieve nobody was taught by); inspector.py gains no forbidden import (tooth 12 — `subprocess` is legal, the forbidden set is network + the `deepen` oracle, VERIFIED by reading the tooth, and git status survives the netns seal because it is local); every existing tooth still greens. Live gate: the sieve fires in anger at a real PROVEME exit with real dirt, and the history stays untouched on the refusal. THE BOUNDARY HALF (skills/saveslate/proofs/): a dirty tree in BOTH roots, fired through the door, leaves both roots clean and pushed and the slate carrying two shas that resolve to commits containing exactly that dirt; a slate written with a wrong template key refuses (the `at_sea`/`in_flight` drift named below was RETIRED BY HAND 2026-07-29 on Akien's ruling — the door's job is to make the schema fire so a sixth-slate drift cannot recur, not to re-decide the term); the door NEVER refuses to write a slate — see falsifier.
falsifier: RED on any of: (1) a clean component draws the new finding (a gate that always fires gets unwired — build_inspector's own tooth 1); (2) seeded dirt fails to red the crossing; (3) the boundary door REFUSES to write a slate on a dirty tree — refusing is the wrong direction: the door commits, it never blocks; (4) the door silently absorbs an untracked file it cannot account for (see the publish constraint in dependencies); (5) a slate lands whose recorded shas do not resolve, or resolve to commits missing the dirt they claim; (6) anything in this stone acquires a clock. THE COMMIT DIRECTION IS RATIFIED (Akien 2026-07-29, resolving the one open assumption in this cast): the 2026-07-29 stop was NOT a deliberate resting state — 'if I didn't stop it when I did, it would have run out of usage within a couple of moments, and it'd be hard stopped then. so if that's the cause of those files, then it had work in progress we should finish.' A dirty tree at a boundary therefore means INTERRUPTED WORK, not preserved work, and the door's job is wider than durability alone: the dirt is a SIGNAL that a voyage is mid-flight, so the slate should derive what is still owed from it rather than depend on a human writing that prose. Retained as a falsifier only in the narrow form: if a future dirty-at-boundary is ever genuinely a raw state Akien wants untouched, the door needs an explicit opt-out, not a reversal.
horizon: re-read when: a third durability event appears (the pattern would then earn a shared shape rather than two sites); the tester lands and the hand-run VALIDATION becomes automatic; CLAUDE.md's 'Rules awaiting physics' section is next edited — the durability IOU is NOT currently listed there (it lives in code-seam.json extra_gates + the /commit charter), and this stone landing is the moment to decide whether that section should have carried it all along.

Inspecting the sail address refuses — 'no component skills/sail under <root>/cairn — the census sees [base, build_inspector, bus, chart, ...]'. So the crossing-half sieve as cast would have ZERO jurisdiction over skills/, which is exactly where the newly-crossing skill class lives, AND over anything else outside cairn/. Two consequences: (1) the crossing half covers strictly less than this ticket assumed at cast, so the boundary half carries more of the load than stated; (2) widening orient's device_census is either a dependency of this stone or a sibling stone in front of it — Akien's call, and it must be settled at constrain, not discovered at build. Do not build the sieve believing it covers skills/.

THE `in_flight`/`at_sea` DIVERGENCE NAMED IN THIS TICKET'S FIRST DRAFT IS SETTLED, and the settling sharpened what the door is for. Two corrections stack. (1) My draft said 'the template names `in_flight`, every real slate writes `at_sea`'. MEASURED at the /sorted pivot the same day: THE CENSUS RAN THE OTHER WAY — 29 slates wrote `in_flight` (the template's own key), 6 wrote `at_sea`, and the `at_sea` ones were the RECENT drift, following skills/saveslate/SKILL.md's prose. So the divergence was SKILL.md vs the template. (2) AKIEN RULED 2026-07-29: 'we should globally rename in_flight to at_sea, simple.' Executed the same day — the template key and 30 slates renamed, 3 prose mentions updated, and the occurrences in cairn/ (5 files, 6 lines: MAP.md:1027 plus harbor_master + web_server history/state) deliberately LEFT because they are the records that EXPLAIN the retirement; sweeping them would erase the history of the rename itself. THE FINDING THAT MATTERS TO THIS STONE: the ruling was not a fresh decision at all but a MISSED MIGRATION — `in_flight` was already retired 2026-07-25 by the build-to-the-tool naming gate ('an AVIATION word inside a nautical system — a ship is never in flight'), the sweep covered code and missed slates/, and the template kept the dead word for four days. So SKILL.md was not drifting; it was CORRECT and out-voted 29-to-6 by a schema nobody validated against. That is precisely the charter's false claim — 'the single commons emit chokepoint validates every record against the template below' — a validation that demonstrably does not fire. A hand-rename fixes the corpus once; only the door firing the schema stops the next retired word from living four days past its gate

PUBLISH CONSTRAINT (bounded, not eliminated): both roots are public on github.com/akienm, so the boundary door's push is an outward act. Bounded BY THE THREE-ROOTS LAW — class-space holds nothing private by construction; credentials, logs and instance state live in ~/.cairn. Residual risk is a stray scratch file, so the door must NAME every untracked file it absorbs in the slate rather than sweeping silently. Push is required, not optional: a local-only commit still dies with the box

chart_notes.constrain: WHICH DIRT HAS A REASON — the sieve must separate accounted-for dirt from loose cargo, and the bound is not obvious. Working proposal: dirt under the crossing component's own subtree, attributable to the crossing ticket, is accounted for; everything else is loose. But stone C spanned cairn/tools/base AND skills/sail, so a per-component sieve crossing one of them is blind to dirt in the other. Settle: does the sieve read the crossing ticket's declared paths, or stay strictly per-subtree and let the boundary door own cross-component dirt? (Strictly per-subtree is the cheaper honest answer — state the limit, do not pretend coverage.)

chart_notes.hypothesize: state as a labelled hypothesis: that a per-component subtree check is sufficient at the crossing. The residue it cannot see — non-component paths (MAP.md, CLAUDE.md, top-level) and cross-component dirt — is the boundary door's jurisdiction, and the boundary is never fired if a session simply ends. THE COVER FOR THAT RESIDUE IS ON-READ, NOT A CLOCK: the session-open read measures both roots and reports before restoring, which is exactly how this bug surfaced by hand on 2026-07-29. UPDATED 2026-07-31: the carrier of that read changed and GOT STRONGER. It was /loadslate, a skill that fired only when Akien typed it; it is now bin/cmd/slate, fired by a checked-in SessionStart hook, so the read is unconditional. That is this stone's own 'on-read, not a clock' principle finally holding by physics rather than by memory — and it does NOT trip falsifier (6), because a hook is an event, not a clock. Bounding the loss window by 'next time anyone touches the system' is the same window in which the work matters

filed_edges: [CORPUS] THE BOUNDARY DOOR HAS A THIRD BEHAVIOUR NOBODY HAS NAMED. Its falsifier reds on REFUSING to write a slate on a dirty tree, and reds on SILENTLY ABSORBING an untracked file it cannot account for. So on an unaccountable untracked file it must neither refuse nor absorb — which leaves a behaviour (report and write? quarantine and write? write and red?) that has not been designed.

[AKIEN] TWO ROOTS, ONE ACT — WHAT IF ONE HALF FAILS? The door measures both roots. If it commits cairn and CairnCommons as one act and the second push fails, the boundary is half-recorded, which is worse than not recorded because it LOOKS closed. Atomicity across two repos is not free and the fallback is a design decision.

SEQUENCING, RULED 2026-08-05 (2026-08-05-filters-become-sieves): this ticket adds a new build_inspector check (working_tree_clean), and the whole family is being renamed sieve -> SIEVE. The rename lands BEFORE this ticket or AFTER it, NEVER DURING — a rename mid-build is how a proof ends up pinning a name that no longer exists. Whichever order, the new check is authored under the surviving word, not migrated across it. RESOLVED 2026-08-06: the rename landed BEFORE, while this ticket sat at TICKETME with nothing in flight — which is the clause honored, not waived. working_tree_clean is therefore authored as a SIEVE from its first line, and it is born with a BAND rather than a position: its reach runs a subprocess over local git, so it derives to correlated-local and shakes after the in-hand checks. Nobody hand-places it; the derivation reads its body (ruling 2026-08-06-a-stack-of-sieves-is-a-nest).
